label: Claude Sonnet 5.5
output:
**Why I'm keeping the busing project**

Jess texted me last night, and I'm paraphrasing only a little: *it's one assignment, don't torch your job over it.* Then a few of you chimed in on the group chat, and most of you were on her side. I get it. I'd probably say the same thing if it were one of you.

I'd rather explain myself once, properly, than do it in fifteen texts where I get defensive and Jess gets patient with me. So this is for all of you, but mostly it's for her.

**What's going on**

For four years I've run the same project in my US History II classes at the high school. I teach juniors, two sections. They interview someone from their family or neighborhood about Boston in 1974 to 1976, the busing and desegregation years. Ten minutes of recording, then a two-page reflection. That's it.

A parent emailed my principal last week and cc'd a school committee member. The email says the project "reopens wounds" and "pressures kids to judge their grandparents." My principal has asked me, in the nicest possible way, to quietly drop it. There's a meeting Thursday, November 19, at 3:15, with him and the parent.

I'm not going to drop it. I'm going to change it, which I'll get to. But I'm keeping it.

**The part where Jess is right**

I want to say this before anything else, because I don't want this to read as me ignoring what you all said. Jess is not wrong. I'm tenured, I've been since 2021, so nobody can just fire me over a project. But my principal still controls my schedule, and he has a lot to say about who gets AP. There are a hundred small ways a job gets worse without anyone ever doing anything you could point to. Jess spent seven years in a building like mine and now works in HR, so she knows that better than most people.

And I'm scared. Not dramatically, but there's a low hum of it, and it's been there since I opened that email. I'm not writing this as someone who feels brave. If I felt brave I'd probably be less careful about it.

**The part where the parent has a point**

I'm not picking a fight with this parent. I mean that. I read the email several times, and one piece of it is true: asking a sixteen-year-old to sit across from their grandmother and ask hard questions about the worst years of the city's history is asking something of them. Some kids will feel pressure. Some will feel it in a way I can't see from the front of the room. "Pressures kids to judge their grandparents" isn't how I'd describe the assignment, because the reflection asks them to understand, not to judge. But I can see how a kid could feel it as judgment, and that's on me to take seriously.

So here's what I'm going to propose Thursday. Nobody has to interview family. A kid can interview a librarian or an archivist who knows the period. Or they can work from the recorded interviews students have done in past years, with permission from the people in them. Same recording, same reflection, same grade. The family interview becomes one option instead of the only one.

That fixes the real problem, which is that a kid could feel trapped. I should have built it that way from the start.

**Why I won't just let it go**

Two stories. Neither is the whole case, but they're why I can't make this one assignment in my head.

In 2023, a student, I'll call him D., interviewed his grandmother. She drove a school bus in Southie in 1974. She had never told anyone in the family about it. Not his mom, not anyone. He found out because I gave him an assignment and he had the nerve to ask her. He played forty seconds of the recording for the class, and when it ended, nobody said a word. For about a minute. I've been teaching for a long time and I can count on one hand the times a room of seventeen-year-olds has been that quiet because they wanted to be.

Last year, a girl interviewed a relative and found out her uncle had thrown rocks at a bus. She was upset. Really upset, not a little uncomfortable. We talked after class twice. And her reflection was the best thing I read all year. It wasn't a tidy "history is complicated" essay. It was a kid working out, on the page, how to hold two true things about someone she loved. I'm not sure she'd have gotten there any other way. I'm also not sure it didn't cost her something, and I think about that.

That's the honest picture. Sometimes it's a gift and sometimes it hurts, and often it's both. Which is exactly why I'm adding the other options and not pretending the hard version is harmless.

**What I actually believe here**

This is the history of the city these kids live in. They walk past the places it happened. Their textbook gives it one paragraph. One. If I drop the project, what I'm really agreeing to is that they get the paragraph and nothing more, and that the people who lived it take the rest of it with them when they go. A lot of those people are in their seventies and eighties now. Nobody is going to ask them later.

And the kids who feel the most uncomfortable are very often the kids who need it most. That's not me being clever about it, it's just what I've seen. The discomfort is usually pointing at something.

But I don't get to force anyone. That's the line, and I think it's the right one. I can build an assignment that makes the hard conversation possible. I can't make a kid have it. Once I add the alternatives, the project stops being something that gets done *to* them and becomes something they choose, and I'm more comfortable defending it that way than I was before the complaint. If that's a good thing that came out of a bad email, fine. I'll take it.

**Jess, specifically**

I know you're not telling me to give up on the idea that this matters. I think you're telling me that being right about something and being safe aren't the same thing, and that I'm allowed to pick safe. You're also saying it because you'd rather have me employed and slightly annoyed than correct and miserable. I know that, and I love you for it.

But I think if I let this go quietly, I'd be teaching something I don't want to teach. That when someone complains, you fold, and that the hard parts of your own city are the first thing to go. I'm not willing to teach that. Not for the price of one uncomfortable meeting.

It might go badly. If it does, I'll tell you, and you can say it. You can even say the whole thing.

**Thursday**

I'll go in at 3:15 with the revised plan, I'll listen to what the parent has to say, and I'll try to be a person and not a position. She might not be won over. That's allowed. I'd still rather she hear the plan from me than a version of it from someone else.

Jess, I'll text you Thursday after the meeting. Whatever happens. You can buy the first round, or I will, depending on how it goes.
